# Where your data lives (and why nothing is backed up) {#sec-storage}

::: {.tldr}
MedicineBow gives you three filesystems: **home** (50 GB, small and precious), **project**
(5 TB, shared with your group, where real datasets and results live), and **scratch** (5 TB,
fast, temporary, purged after 90 days of inactivity). **None of them is backed up.** Install
software into `/project/<proj>/software`, not home — one conda env can fill your entire home
directory.
:::

## The single most important sentence in this book

> **Nothing on MedicineBow is backed up. Not home, not project, not scratch.**

There *are* snapshots (point-in-time copies you can sometimes restore from), but snapshots
live on the **same storage array** as your live data. If that array fails, the snapshots
fail with it. Snapshots protect you from *"I accidentally deleted that file yesterday"* —
they do **not** protect you from hardware loss. Anything you cannot afford to lose must have
a copy somewhere else (your institution's storage, a cloud bucket, the separate **Alcova**
service which *does* have real nightly backups, etc.).

Internalize this before you generate a month of simulation output onto scratch and assume
it's safe.

## The three filesystems

| Path | Quota | Snapshots | Backups | Purged |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `/home/$USER` | **50 GB** | yes | **NO** | only when you leave UW |
| `/project/<proj>` | **5 TB** | yes | **NO** | 6 months after project ends |
| `/gscratch/$USER` (`$SCRATCH`) | **5 TB** | yes | **NO** | **after 90 days of inactivity** |
| `/project/<proj>/software` | **+250 GB** on top of project | yes | **NO** | with the project |
| `/lscratch` | node-local, varies | no | **NO** | **wiped at the end of every job** |

Check where you stand at any time:

```bash
arccquota
```

which prints your usage and limits for home, scratch, and project side by side.

### `/home` — small, personal, for config not data

50 GB sounds like a lot until your first conda environment eats 15 GB of it. Home is for
dotfiles, scripts, small configs — **not** datasets and **not** software installs. When home
fills up, weird things break (jobs fail to write logs, logins misbehave), so keep an eye on
it with `arccquota` and `du -sh ~/* | sort -h`.

### `/project/<proj>` — the shared workhorse

5 TB, shared by everyone on your project (e.g. `cowy-firesurro`). This is where shared
datasets, inputs, and results belong. Because it's shared, agree on a directory convention
with your group so you don't clobber each other. It persists for 6 months after the project
formally ends — long enough to get your data out, not a permanent archive.

### `/gscratch/$USER` — fast and disposable

Also 5 TB, and this is the **fast** filesystem — use it as the working directory for running
jobs that do heavy I/O. The catch is in the name: it's *scratch*. Files untouched for **90
days** are purged automatically. Never keep the only copy of anything here.

::: {.callout-note}
## Is it 45 days or 90? It's 90.
The legacy Confluence docs say scratch is purged after 45 days of inactivity. The current
ARCC wiki says 90. Both pages are live on the web, which is confusing — but **90 is the
current policy.** Either way: don't treat scratch as storage.
:::

### `/lscratch` — node-local, gone when the job ends

Each compute node has its own local disk mounted at `/lscratch`. It's the fastest storage
available to a job (no network in the way), which makes it ideal for scratch files a single
job reads and rewrites constantly. But it is **wiped the instant your job ends**, so copy
anything you want to keep back to `/project` or `/gscratch` *before* your job exits.

(There is no `/data` filesystem, despite what some docs suggest — it doesn't exist on the
machine.)

## The #1 self-inflicted wound: installing software into home

::: {.callout-important}
## Install software into `/project/<proj>/software`, not `/home`
Your project has an extra **250 GB** quota specifically at `/project/<proj>/software` for
installing software — and ARCC wants you to use it. A single conda environment with a few
scientific packages can be 10–20 GB. Put two of those in your 50 GB home directory and
you're full, with mysterious failures everywhere.

Point conda, pip, R libraries, and manual builds at project software space from the start.
The conda chapter (@sec-conda) shows exactly how.
:::

## A sane layout to adopt on day one

```text
/home/<you>/                      # dotfiles, small scripts, SSH keys
/project/cowy-firesurro/
    software/                     # conda envs, container images, manual builds
    data/                         # shared input datasets
    <you>/                        # your working area within the project
/gscratch/<you>/                  # active job working dirs, heavy I/O, big temp output
```

With storage sorted, the next question is how to get data *into* these filesystems — which
is @sec-moving-data.
